result.summary: Pausanias describes the temple of Hera at Olympia and the quadrennial festival in which sixteen matrons weave a robe and oversee a girls' footrace. He gives the traditions of its origin with Hippodamia, the matrons' role in settling the quarrel with Pisa, and the dances of Physcoa and Hippodamia.

scenes.title: The temple of Hera
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Doric temple, its date of building, its oak pillar and size.

scenes.title: The Hera festival and maidens' race
scenes.summary: Sixteen matrons weave a robe and run the girls' footraces; victors receive olive crowns and a share of the heifer.

scenes.title: Hippodamia founds the games
scenes.summary: The Eleans say Hippodamia thanked Hera for her marriage to Pelops by founding the games; Chloris won.

scenes.title: Damophon and the sixteen cities
scenes.summary: After the tyrant Damophon's injuries, sixteen cities each chose a matron to arbitrate peace with Pisa; they later ran the festival.
scenes.stakes: Peace between Elis and Pisa after the tyrant's wrongs.

scenes.title: Physcoa and her dance
scenes.summary: Physcoa of Elis bore Narcaeus to Dionysus; he built a temple of Athene Narcaea and they first worshipped Dionysus.

scenes.title: Later matrons and lustration
scenes.summary: Two matrons are now chosen from each of eight tribes, and rites begin with a pig sacrifice and washing at the fountain Piera.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid detail of the runners' dress and loose hair at the Heraean games.

analysis.text: The Heraean games were a women's athletic festival alongside the men's Olympics, showing female ritual roles in Elis.
Pausanias links ritual practices to rival local traditions, explaining customs through myth and politics.

legacy.text: The Heraean games are often cited as the earliest known organised women's athletic competition in Greece.

fun_facts.text: The Heraion at Olympia is one of the oldest known Doric temples; Pausanias saw one original oak pillar still standing.

language_notes.text: Oxylus was the Aetolian leader who, in legend, became king of Elis after the Dorian invasion; the date is counted from his accession.
"Shawl" translates the peplos, a woven robe offered to the goddess. Every fifth year means the four-year cycle counted inclusively.
A stade was the length of the Olympic track, about 600 Greek feet (roughly 190 metres); the maidens' course was one sixth shorter.
Chloris was a daughter of Amphion and Niobe; most of Niobe's children were killed by Apollo and Artemis. Her original name was Meliboea.
"Annul their charges" means the Eleans were willing to drop their claims against Pisa, since the Pisans had not officially approved Damophon's crimes.
"Told off" is old-fashioned for appointed or assigned to a task.
"Parish" renders a local district or township; Orthia was a locality in Elis.
"Lustration" is ritual purification, here by washing with water.
"Umpires of Elis" are the Hellanodicae, the judges who presided over the Olympic games.

context_notes.text: Doric is the plainest Greek architectural order, with sturdy fluted columns. An oak pillar surviving in the rear chamber suggests the temple's very early, wooden origins.
Hippodamia won Pelops as husband after he defeated her father Oenomaus in a chariot race. Pelops gave his name to the Peloponnese.
The Heraea was a festival with footraces for girls at Olympia; the robe woven for Hera's image was a main offering.
Dionysus is the god of wine and ecstatic worship; Athene is the goddess of wisdom and war, so the temple title Narcæa honours Narcæus.
Olympia lay in the territory once held by Pisa, and Elis was the city that came to control the games.

literary_notes.text: The traveller-historian's candid admission of missing information shows his careful, source-conscious tone.
Pausanias links this passage to his earlier Argos account, giving the work a connected, encyclopedic structure.
Repeated "the tradition goes" and "they say" show Pausanias distancing himself from the story, reporting local belief without vouching for it.
The curt closing line shows the writer's authority as eyewitness, ending the digression with a plain assertion of accuracy.
